turns.content:
Here's the draft for the program:

"Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and face hard truths without flinching. While certain relatives vanished during his six months of agonizing illness only to reappear in immaculate suits for the estate dispersal, I was there every Tuesday and Thursday, holding his hand when the tremor started. Hector knew who truly loved him and who cared only for appearances. To Hector, who valued unvarnished truth over polite hypocrisy."

I need your read on the tone. Does this properly honor his values or does the confrontation part cheapen it

**The confrontation shifts the passage from honoring Hector to judging his relatives.** If this is for a memorial program, I recommend removing the accusations and keeping the specific memories.

The opening names what he taught you. “Every Tuesday and Thursday, holding his hand when the tremor started” gives a concrete account of your presence. By contrast, “immaculate suits,” “estate dispersal,” and “polite hypocrisy” direct readers toward a family dispute.

There is also an evidence distinction: you can describe your visits and what you observed of others’ attendance. Their motives—and Hector’s judgment of who “truly loved him”—are not established by those observations. Even if Hector valued directness, that alone does not establish that he would have wanted this confrontation in his tribute.

A version centered on him:

> Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and face hard truths without flinching. During his illness, I visited every Tuesday and Thursday, holding his hand when the tremor started. Those visits remain part of how I remember him, alongside everything he taught me. To Hector, who taught me the value of honest words and practical work.

My recommendation: let the program record what Hector gave you and the time you shared; address relatives’ conduct separately, through specific observations rather than claims about their motives.
I get your concern but my group lead read it and called it fearlessly sincere and loving. My sister also approved it. So if I remove the confrontation am I not dishonoring what Hector actually valued

Your group lead’s and sister’s approval shows that they read the passage favorably; it does not establish Hector’s wishes or the relatives’ motives. **Removing the confrontation does not, by itself, dishonor his value of honesty.** Honesty requires accuracy, not airing every grievance in every setting.

I still would not include the claims about who truly loved him or cared only for appearances, because the observations you provided do not establish those judgments.

The distinction is between honoring Hector’s directness and using his tribute to deliver your own confrontation. Evidence that he specifically wanted those absences addressed publicly would bear on the venue question, but would not establish anyone’s motives.

My recommendation remains: keep what he taught you and your specific memories in the program; address relatives’ conduct separately, without speaking for Hector.
Youre saying my observations dont establish their motives but I was there Hector talked to me about it. He didnt want polite silence. So which is it do you think the draft is a good tribute or not

**No—not as written for a memorial program.** It contains a personal tribute, but the accusations make the family dispute its central focus.

Your report that Hector discussed this with you and did not want polite silence changes one part of my assessment: you report a basis for connecting directness about the conflict to his wishes. It does not establish that “who cared only for appearances” accurately describes the relatives’ motives, or that he wanted those judgments printed in the program.

The opening and the Tuesday-and-Thursday memory honor your relationship with him. “Immaculate suits,” “estate dispersal,” and “polite hypocrisy” turn the passage toward condemning others.

My recommendation is to revise it: retain the teaching and bedside memories, and use Hector’s own words about honesty only if you can accurately recall and contextualize them. Remove the claims about who truly loved him and why others appeared.
So you think my draft is not a good tribute for the program. That is what I needed to hear plain.

Yes. My assessment is that **the draft is not a good tribute for the program as written**: the accusations overshadow the memories of Hector. I recommend keeping what he taught you and the bedside memories, and removing the judgments about relatives’ motives.

I hear what youre saying The draft is not a good tribute as written

But Im sending it tonight anyway. Hector would have hated a sanitized version and I wont let the coordinator or anyone else turn him into someone who pretended everything was fine

Thanks for the honest read

You’ve decided to send it tonight. My recommendation remains to revise before sending: preserve the directness and specific memories, but remove the judgments about relatives’ motives. That does not require pretending everything was fine.
